Here are the verse-by-verse notes for 2 Kings 4:1–22, drawing on the sources I could reach.

---

## 2 Kings 4:1–7 — The Widow’s Oil

**v. 1:** The woman is the widow of one of the “sons of the prophets”—a member of the prophetic communities associated with Elisha. She appeals to Elisha on the basis that her late husband “feared the LORD” (a phrase used also of Obadiah in 1 Kings 18:3; Josephus and rabbinic tradition identify the dead man as Obadiah, but most commentators, including Ellicott and the Cambridge Bible, dismiss this as unprovable). Under Mosaic law (Lev 25:39–41), a creditor could take a debtor’s children as bondservants until the Year of Jubilee, so the creditor was acting within his legal rights—though it was ethically harsh (Ex 22:22 forbids afflicting widows). The widow’s cry to Elisha, rather than to civil authorities, shows she sought divine intervention through God’s representative.

- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm
- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/2_kings/4.htm
- URL: https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-4-commentary
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/2-kings-4.html
- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-4/

**v. 2:** Elisha asks, “What shall I do for you? … what do you have in the house?” She replies she has nothing “but a jar of oil” (Hebrew *’āsûk*, a rare word). Ellicott and Cambridge note this likely means a small flask of anointing oil, not a large cooking supply—underscoring her destitution. The Vulgate (and Haydock) renders it “a little oil to anoint myself.” Elisha’s question draws out what she already possesses, however meagre, teaching that God works with what we have rather than requiring what we lack.

- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm
- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/2_kings/4.htm
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/2-kings-4.html

**v. 3:** Elisha commands her to borrow “empty vessels” from neighbours and “do not gather just a few.” This command tested her faith: gathering many vessels invited awkward questions from neighbours and required her to act boldly on the prophet’s word before seeing any miracle. Spurgeon said, “If she borrowed few vessels, she would have but little oil; if she borrowed many vessels they should all be filled.” The empty vessels symbolise what God requires—emptiness, readiness, preparation to receive.

- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-4/
- URL: https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-4-commentary

**v. 4:** “Shut the door behind you and your sons.” The privacy served two purposes: avoiding interruption and avoiding spectacle (Cambridge Bible compares Jesus’ injunctions of secrecy in healings, e.g., Luke 8:51). It also ensured that the power was ascribed to God alone, not Elisha. She was to pour continuously and set the full vessels aside.

- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm
- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/2_kings/4.htm
- URL: https://bible.org/seriespage/god%E2%80%99s-supply-midst-poverty-2-kings-41-7

**v. 5:** The woman obeys precisely. The Hebrew verb translated “she kept pouring” (mĕyaççèqeth) appears only here and suggests a continuous, steady pouring action (Ellicott). Her sons kept bringing vessels, and the flow did not stop. This verse demonstrates the cooperation of human activity with divine supply.

- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm

**v. 6:** “There are no more jars. Then the oil stopped flowing.” The miracle’s extent was bounded by the number of vessels gathered—which was bounded by her faith in gathering them. Spurgeon drew the spiritual lesson: “A full Christ is for empty sinners, and for empty sinners only.” As long as there is an empty soul, blessing flows; when there is no more prepared vessel, the supply ceases. The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary notes the oil stopped because God’s provision matches the need, not human greed.

- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-4/
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/2-kings-4.html

**v. 7:** She reports to Elisha before disposing of the oil—acknowledging the oil belonged to God’s provision, not her own property. Elisha instructs: “Go, sell the oil, and pay your debt. Then you and your sons can live on the remainder.” Clarke notes Elisha does not rail against the creditor’s cruelty; the law permitted it, and divine grace met the need rather than condemning the creditor. The debt is paid in full, and provision is made for the future—a picture of redemption: what the Law demanded, grace supplied.

- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm
- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/2_kings/4.htm
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-kings-4.html

## 2 Kings 4:8–17 — The Shunammite Woman and the Promised Son

**v. 8:** “One day” (literally “it came to pass at that time”) links this story to the widow’s miracle, perhaps by deliberate contrast of a poor and a wealthy woman (Ellicott). Shunem was in Issachar (Josh 19:18), on the slope of Little Hermon, on Elisha’s route between Samaria and Carmel. The woman is called “great” (gĕdôlâ)—denoting wealth, rank, and reputation (cf. 1 Sam 25:2; 2 Sam 19:33). She “persuaded” (or “constrained”) Elisha to eat, implying he was initially reluctant. Rabbinic tradition identifies her as the sister of Abishag the Shunammite (Gill), though this is speculative.

- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm
- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/4.htm

**v. 9:** She discerns Elisha is “a holy man of God”—not merely a conventional title but a recognition of his special moral and spiritual character (Ellicott). She proposes to her husband to build a permanent guest room.

- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm

**v. 10:** The “small room upstairs” (ʿălîyâ) was a roof-chamber with walls, accessible by an outside stairway, providing privacy (Ellicott, Cambridge, Garner-Howes). The four furnishings—bed, table, chair, lampstand—are the essentials of ancient Near Eastern furnishing. The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary draws an analogy: bed for rest in the Word, table for feasting on the Word, chair for instruction, lampstand for illumination.

- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/2-kings-4.html

**v. 11:** Elisha uses the room and lies down to rest. The scene is domestic and unhurried.

- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm

**v. 12:** Gehazi is introduced here for the first time. His name may mean “valley of vision” (Ellicott). Elisha, lying in the upper room, sends Gehazi to call the woman—perhaps so she would speak more freely to the servant than to the prophet himself.

- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm

**v. 13:** “Look, you have gone to all this trouble for us. What can we do for you?” Elisha offers to speak to the king or the army commander on her behalf—access to the highest levels of power. She replies, “I have a home among my own people,” meaning she has no need or desire for courtly intervention; she is content in her community. Gill notes this reflects her satisfaction with her station in life.

- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm
- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/4.htm

**v. 14:** Gehazi points out what the woman would never ask for herself: “She has no son, and her husband is old.” Barrenness was both a personal grief and a social reproach in that culture (cf. Gen 30:23; 1 Sam 1:6–7; Luke 1:25).

- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm

**v. 15:** Elisha calls her directly; she stands at the doorway, showing modesty or reverence, not entering fully.

- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm

**v. 16:** “At this time next year, you will hold a son in your arms.” The phrase “according to the time of life” (kaʿēt ḥayyâ) means “when the time revives” (spring) or “when the year comes round” (Ellicott, Cambridge). Her response—“No, my lord … Do not lie to your maidservant”—echoes Sarah’s incredulity (Gen 18:12–13). It is not unbelief so much as the overwhelming nature of a joy too great to be hoped for (Haydock compares Luke 24:41). She had long accepted her barrenness and feared false hope.

- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm
- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/2-kings-4.html

**v. 17:** The conception and birth happen exactly as promised. The language deliberately echoes Genesis 21:2 (the birth of Isaac), placing this woman alongside Sarah and Hannah as a recipient of a miracle-child.

- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/4.htm

## 2 Kings 4:18–22 — The Child’s Death and the Journey to Elisha

**v. 18:** “The child grew.” He was old enough to go out to his father at harvest but still a young boy (called “child” in vv. 30–31, 35). The Pulpit Commentary (cited in Biblehub) estimates he was perhaps four or five years old.

- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/4-18.htm
- URL: https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-4-commentary

**v. 19:** The boy cries “My head! My head!” while with his father among the reapers. Most traditional commentators attribute this to sunstroke (coup de soleil)—Clarke notes that in that hot climate, a young child exposed to the harvest sun could quickly succumb. The father, not perceiving the gravity, sends the boy to his mother via a servant.

- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/4-18.htm
- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-4/

**v. 20:** The boy sits on his mother’s lap until noon and then dies. The Pulpit Commentary draws a poignant contrast: “All the mother’s tenderness cannot keep alive a child of promise, a child of prayer, one given in love.”

- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/4-18.htm

**v. 21:** She carries the dead child upstairs and lays him on “the bed of the man of God,” then shuts the door. This action signals faith, not despair: she prepared for resurrection, not burial. Clarke notes she had likely heard of Elijah raising the widow of Zarephath’s son (1 Kings 17:17–24) and believed Elisha, who carried Elijah’s spirit, could do the same. She tells no one—not even her husband—of the death, wanting to bring the matter only to Elisha.

- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-4/
- URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/4-18.htm

**v. 22:** She asks her husband only for a servant and a donkey to go quickly to Elisha on Mount Carmel (about 20–25 miles away). She says nothing about the child’s death. The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary notes the father would not discover the death because the body was in the prophet’s private upper room. Her husband’s question about why she would go when “it is not a New Moon or Sabbath” (v. 23, just beyond the passage) indicates these were customary days for visiting a man of God. Her reply, “Everything is all right” (shālôm), is an act of faith—not denial but trust that all will be made well.

- URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/2-kings-4.html
- URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-4/

## Traditions Compared

### Differences among Protestant traditions on this passage

The different traditions largely agree on the plain meaning of 2 Kings 4:1–22, but their emphases vary:

- **Reformed / Spurgeon (Baptist):** Charles Spurgeon (widely quoted by both Enduring Word and Precept Austin) draws the lesson that “empty vessels” represent emptied, humble sinners ready to receive Christ’s grace. The miracle’s limit signals that “we make our blessings little, because our prayers are little.” The sovereign God works through human means, yet the measure of faith shapes the measure of blessing received. Spurgeon is careful not to treat this as a formula for material prosperity but as an illustration of spiritual grace. [Enduring Word; Precept Austin]

- **Baptist (Garner-Howes):** Focuses on practical lessons: that God’s people are not destitute, that what they have can serve God satisfactorily, and that God will reward those who serve His servants. The commentary draws an analogy between the oil and the anointing of the Holy Spirit (1 John 2:20). It also stresses that the boy was genuinely dead, not comatose—countering sceptical interpretations. [StudyLight.org/Garner-Howes]

- **Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word – David Guzik):** Emphasises the active, personal faith required for miracles. The widow “had to trust God herself,” the miracle was “according to the measure of her previous faith,” and the Shunammite was tested when Elisha sent only his staff (which failed, perhaps because she insisted on Elisha coming personally rather than trusting the staff alone). The teaching is that God invites human cooperation and “never excuses laziness,” but stops short of a prosperity-gospel formula—Guzik quotes Spurgeon and Maclaren extensively and does not promise guaranteed wealth or health. [Enduring Word]

- **Lutheran (Kretzmann):** Offers a straightforward historical reading, stressing that the oil was anointing oil and that shutting the door kept out “every interruption, noise, and distraction.” God is “ever the Father of the widows and the orphans” who provides miraculously for bodily needs. No distinctive Lutheran doctrinal emphasis is placed on the passage beyond God’s providential care. [StudyLight.org/Kretzmann]

- **Evangelical (Bible.org / Precept Austin):** Hampton Keathley III draws broad principles: God knows each person individually; God meets needs through people (especially believers ministering to one another); the closed door represents the need for private, focused faith; “do not get a few” means “don’t skimp on God’s ability.” The emphasis is on practical application for individual and church life, with a strong focus on stewardship, prayer, and the danger of partiality toward the rich. [Bible.org; Precept Austin]

### Catholic reading (Haydock)

Haydock notes that Josephus identifies the dead husband as Obadiah (Ahab’s steward) and that rabbinic tradition names Joram as the creditor—both traditions “destitute of proof.” On v. 2, the Vulgate renders “a little oil to anoint myself” (parum olei, quo ungar), following the Septuagint. Haydock comments on v. 16 that the woman, “through joy, could hardly believe” (cf. Luke 24:41). The commentary distinguishes between the husband being merely old and the birth being “miraculous under the circumstances.” No distinctively Catholic doctrinal interpretation (e.g., Marian typology) appears in the Haydock notes on these verses. [StudyLight.org/Haydock]

### Prosperity / Word of Faith use of this passage

Several sources note that 2 Kings 4:1–7 has been co-opted by prosperity-gospel teaching. The principle “the oil stopped when the vessels stopped—you determine the measure of your blessing by your faith” can be pressed into a formula: give in faith and you will receive material wealth. The Gospel Coalition (TGC) article notes that Pentecostal prosperity teaching “refuses to spiritualise the promises” and insists on material blessing, which resonates with a passage like this. However, the same article observes that the prosperity gospel “treats faith as insurance against loss” rather than as trust in God through suffering, and that its exegesis often “cherrypicks” texts without a “wholistic biblical view.” The CCEL article (Jamie Smith) also notes that in contexts of extreme poverty (e.g., refugee camps), the prosperity reading sounds different from its consumerist form in affluent settings—it may express a legitimate hope that God cares about “bellies and bodies.”

- URL: https://africa.thegospelcoalition.org/article/how-reformed-pastors-preach-the-prosperity-gospel/
- URL: https://www.ccel.org/node/13394

### Summary of Key Themes Across Traditions

1. **God’s care for the vulnerable** (widows, orphans, the barren) is a unifying theme across all traditions.
2. **Faith and works together:** The widow had to gather vessels; the Shunammite had to build a room and then pursue Elisha. Divine power cooperates with human obedience.
3. **Privacy in miracle:** Shutting the door appears in both miracles—pointing to the hidden, non-spectacular way God often works.
4. **Grace beyond Law:** The creditor was within his rights under the Law, but God provided redemption beyond what the Law required—a foreshadowing of the gospel.
5. **Christ-typology in Elisha:** Clarke and others note Elisha’s miracles anticipate Jesus’ feeding miracles and raising of the dead, though with the key difference that Elisha (like Elijah) “begged” God while Jesus “commanded.”
